content:
San Antonio has an accountability problem. Consider two issues that seem worlds apart: the unruly conduct of some council members and the city’s struggle to protect residents from disastrous flooding. At first glance, they have little in common. One involves individual behavior; the other involves engineering, infrastructure and billions of dollars. But, both scenarios reveal that no one is responsible when something goes wrong; there is just superficial outrage and social media spectacle.

Three council members — Clayton Perry, Marc Whyte and most recently, Ivalis Meza-Gonzalez — have faced driving while intoxicated arrests or charges over the past four years. Perry was arrested in November 2022 after a motor vehicle crash and was charged with DWI and failure to stop and provide information. Whyte was arrested in December 2023 on suspicion of DWI; though, his case was later resolved through a plea to obstruction of a highway, with deferred adjudication. In July 2025, Meza-Gonzalez was arrested on a DWI charge.

These cases involve different circumstances and outcomes, and they should not be treated as if they are identical, nor do they prove corruption or definitive incompetence. However, they raise a serious question about standards. When these acts of misconduct occur, members are often met with a censure. A censure vote is what the city council resorts to when a member’s actions are so reprehensible it calls for a public condemnation. Their voting power does not get taken away and they do not lose any power. Accountability cannot mean simply expressing symbolic outrage after something controversial happens; it must mean setting standards, consequences, corrections and measurable results.

The same principle applies to flooding.

On June 12, 2025, catastrophic flooding killed 13 people in the San Antonio area. More than six inches of rain fell. A city-commissioned Kleinfelder report found that 2022 flood models underestimated the water that could move through a water crossing. According to Kleinfelder Program Manager Justin Murray, dense vegetation and limited technology were the main reasons that predictions failed. The City Council does not design every drainage channel or inspect every culvert. San Antonio’s council-manager system gives professional staff “substantial responsibility,” but professional responsibility cannot become an accountability black hole.

The council sets priorities, approves budgets and bonds, receives reports and holds hearings. When systems fail, elected officials must ask why. Accountability cannot end with blame. It must produce standards, consequences, corrections and results. After repeated conduct controversies and deadly floods, the city council needs to improve and produce measurable results for its citizens.
